title: The Power of Positive Emotions in Occupational Stress Coping: A Social/Positive Psychology Approach
content: Purpose: Occupational stress remains one of the most significant psychosocial challenges affecting employee well-being and organizational effectiveness worldwide. Although extensive research has examined the detrimental effects of workplace stress, less attention has been devoted to the protective role of positive emotional experiences. Drawing upon Positive Psychology and Fredrickson’s Broaden-and-Build Theory, the present study investigates the contribution of positive emotions to occupational stress coping within a large Greek workforce sample. Methodology: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 2,614 Greek employees from both public and private sector organizations. Participants completed validated measures assessing occupational stress, positive emotions, negative emotions, dispositional optimism, and demographic and occupational characteristics. Correlational analyses, analysis of variance, partial correlations, and advanced explanatory modeling approaches were employed to examine the relationships between positive emotional experiences and occupational stress. Findings: Results demonstrated a significant negative association between positive emotions and occupational stress (r = -.39, p < .001). The ratio of positive to negative emotions emerged as an even stronger predictor of stress reduction (r = -.53, p < .001). Employees experiencing high levels of positive emotions reported substantially lower stress scores compared with employees experiencing predominantly negative emotional states. Furthermore, the observed relationships remained statistically significant after controlling for eleven demographic, occupational, and health-related variables. Dispositional optimism emerged as the most influential moderating factor. Originality: The study contributes to the occupational stress literature by highlighting the central role of positive emotional experiences as psychological resources that facilitate stress coping and resilience. The findings support contemporary positive psychology models suggesting that flourishing employees are better equipped to manage occupational demands. Practical Implications: Organizations may reduce occupational stress through interventions aimed at strengthening positive emotions, psychological resilience, optimism, and employee well-being.
